We present new predictions for the galaxy three-point correlation function (3PCF) using high-resolution dissipationless cosmological simulations of a flat LCDM Universe which resolve galaxy-size halos and subhalos. We create realistic mock galaxy catalogs by assigning luminosities and colors to dark matter halos and subhalos, and we measure the reduced 3PCF as a function of luminosity and color in both real and redshift space. As galaxy luminosity and color are varied, we find small differences in the amplitude and shape dependence of the reduced 3PCF, at a level qualitatively consistent with recent measurements from the SDSS and 2dFGRS. We confirm that discrepancies between previous 3PCF measurements can be explained in part by differences in binning choices. We explore the degree to which a simple local bias model can fit the simulated 3PCF. The agreement between the model predictions and galaxy 3PCF measurements lends further credence to the straightforward association of galaxies with CDM halos and subhalos.

# Galaxy Three-Point Correlation Functions from High-Resolution Cosmological Simulations

## Simulation Methodology

Researchers employed high-resolution, dissipationless cosmological simulations to model a flat Lambda Cold Dark Matter (ΛCDM) universe, generating new theoretical predictions for the galaxy three-point correlation function (3PCF). These simulations were specifically designed with sufficient resolution to resolve individual galaxy-size dark matter halos as well as their associated subhalos—a critical requirement for accurately modeling the small-scale clustering properties of galaxies and connecting theoretical predictions directly to observable galaxy populations.

## Mock Catalog Construction and Measurements

To bridge the gap between dark matter simulations and observable galaxy properties, the research team constructed realistic mock galaxy catalogs by assigning luminosities and colors to the identified dark matter halos and subhalos. This approach allowed for a direct measurement of the reduced 3PCF as a function of these key galaxy properties. Importantly, these measurements were carried out in both real space and redshift space, enabling a more comprehensive comparison with observational surveys that inherently measure clustering in redshift space due to peculiar velocity distortions.

## Dependence on Galaxy Properties

The analysis revealed that variations in galaxy luminosity and color introduce only modest differences in both the amplitude and the shape dependence of the reduced 3PCF. These subtle variations are qualitatively consistent with recent observational measurements from major galaxy surveys, including the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) and the Two-degree Field Galaxy Redshift Survey (2dFGRS). This agreement lends support to the simulation framework's ability to capture the essential physics governing how galaxy properties correlate with higher-order clustering statistics.

## Resolving Discrepancies in Previous Measurements

A significant outcome of this work is the confirmation that inconsistencies among earlier 3PCF measurements from different observational studies can be partially attributed to methodological differences—specifically, the choice of binning schemes used in the various analyses. This finding helps reconcile apparent tensions in the literature and underscores the importance of carefully matched analysis techniques when comparing 3PCF results across different studies or between simulations and observations.

## Testing the Local Bias Model

Finally, the researchers tested a simple local bias model against the 3PCF measurements derived from their simulations. The strong level of agreement found between this model's predictions and the measured galaxy 3PCF provides compelling support for the physical picture in which galaxies are directly associated with cold dark matter (CDM) halos and their subhalos. This result reinforces the validity of using halo-based bias models to describe the relationship between galaxy clustering and the underlying dark matter distribution, offering a robust theoretical foundation for interpreting galaxy survey data in the context of structure formation.

# Galaxy Three-Point Correlation Functions from High-Resolution ΛCDM Simulations

## Introduction and Motivation

The three-point correlation function (3PCF) provides a powerful statistical tool for probing the non-Gaussian features of the galaxy distribution that remain hidden to two-point statistics alone. While the two-point correlation function (2PCF) has been extensively used to constrain cosmological parameters and galaxy bias models, the 3PCF carries complementary information about the higher-order clustering of matter and, crucially, about how galaxies populate dark matter halos. Recent large redshift surveys such as the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) and the Two-degree Field Galaxy Redshift Survey (2dFGRS) have enabled precise measurements of the 3PCF as a function of galaxy luminosity and color, revealing clustering trends that any successful galaxy formation model must reproduce.

## Methodology

In this study, we address the galaxy 3PCF using a suite of high-resolution, dissipationless ΛCDM cosmological N-body simulations. The simulations are designed with sufficient mass and force resolution to resolve galaxy-sized dark matter halos and their embedded substructure (subhalos) down to scales relevant for individual galaxy formation. This resolution is essential because it allows us to move beyond simple halo occupation distribution (HOD) prescriptions and instead directly identify dark matter subhalos as the hosts of individual galaxies, including satellite galaxies residing within larger host halos.

Using the halo and subhalo catalogs extracted from the simulations, we construct realistic mock galaxy catalogs by assigning luminosities and colors to each halo/subhalo according to prescriptions calibrated to match observed luminosity functions and color distributions from SDSS and 2dFGRS. This approach—often referred to as "subhalo abundance matching" or related techniques—preserves the full spatial and kinematic information of the dark matter substructure, allowing us to naturally capture the relationship between galaxy properties and their host halo environment.

We then measure the reduced 3PCF, Q, for these mock catalogs in both real space and redshift space, the latter incorporating the effects of peculiar velocities to enable direct comparison with observational data drawn from spectroscopic surveys. To interpret our results within a theoretical framework, we test a simple local bias model, in which the galaxy density field is expressed as a local, deterministic function of the underlying matter density field characterized by linear and quadratic bias parameters (b₁ and b₂). This model provides a means to connect the higher-order clustering statistics to the physics of galaxy bias in a straightforward and interpretable manner.

## Results

Our analysis reveals clear luminosity- and color-dependent variations in the reduced 3PCF: more luminous and redder galaxies exhibit systematically different Q values compared to fainter, bluer galaxies, mirroring the dependencies observed in the SDSS and 2dFGRS datasets. These trends arise naturally from the resolved subhalo population without the need for additional free parameters beyond the luminosity and color assignment scheme, lending strong support to the physical picture in which galaxy formation is intimately tied to halo and subhalo assembly.

Furthermore, our results help clarify the origin of previously reported discrepancies between different observational 3PCF measurements. We demonstrate that many of these apparent inconsistencies stem not from genuine differences in the underlying galaxy clustering but rather from methodological choices, particularly the specific binning schemes used to compute triangle configurations in the 3PCF estimators. When measurements are compared using consistent binning strategies, the various observational results converge, and our simulated mock catalogs match them well.

## Conclusions

Overall, our simulations achieve strong quantitative agreement with the observed 3PCF across a range of luminosities, colors, and triangle shapes and scales, in both real and redshift space. This concordance between ΛCDM-based mock catalogs—constructed by directly associating galaxies with resolved dark matter halos and subhalos—and observational data reinforces the validity of this approach for galaxy clustering studies. Our results demonstrate that higher-order clustering statistics, and not just the 2PCF, can be successfully reproduced within the standard ΛCDM paradigm when galaxy formation is modeled through the direct link between luminous galaxies and the nonlinear dark matter substructure they inhabit. This validates the use of high-resolution N-body simulations combined with subhalo-based galaxy assignment as a robust tool for interpreting and predicting higher-order galaxy clustering statistics in current and future galaxy surveys.

# The Lambda-CDM Model and Large-Scale Structure: Insights from the SDSS

The Lambda Cold Dark Matter (ΛCDM) model stands as the prevailing cosmological framework for understanding the origin, evolution, and large-scale structure of the Universe. This model combines two fundamental components: dark energy, represented by the cosmological constant (Λ), which drives the accelerated expansion of the Universe, and cold dark matter (CDM), an invisible substance that interacts gravitationally but not electromagnetically. Together with ordinary baryonic matter, these components account for the observed dynamics and structure formation across cosmic history.

According to ΛCDM, the Universe began with a hot, dense state approximately 13.8 billion years ago. Tiny quantum fluctuations, imprinted during an early period of cosmic inflation, seeded the gravitational collapse of matter into the vast cosmic web we observe today—a network of galaxy clusters, filaments, and voids. Dark matter, comprising roughly 27% of the Universe's total energy density, provides the gravitational scaffolding necessary for these structures to form, while dark energy, making up about 68%, governs the Universe's expansion rate at later epochs.

The Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) has played an instrumental role in testing and refining the ΛCDM model. Launched in 2000, SDSS has mapped millions of galaxies and quasars, creating one of the most detailed three-dimensional maps of the Universe ever produced. By measuring the redshifts and spatial distribution of galaxies across vast cosmic volumes, SDSS has provided critical observational evidence supporting key predictions of ΛCDM, including the statistical properties of the cosmic web and the characteristic clustering scale known as baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO).

BAO measurements, in particular, serve as a "standard ruler" for cosmological distances, allowing researchers to trace the expansion history of the Universe with remarkable precision. SDSS data, particularly from its Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey (BOSS) and extended BOSS (eBOSS) programs, have refined constraints on cosmological parameters such as the Hubble constant, the matter density parameter, and the equation of state of dark energy, all of which are central to the ΛCDM framework.

Despite its remarkable success in explaining a wide range of observations—from the cosmic microwave background to large-scale structure—the ΛCDM model faces ongoing challenges. Tensions between different measurements of the Hubble constant (the so-called "Hubble tension") and discrepancies in structure growth rates (the "S8 tension") have prompted cosmologists to scrutinize the model's assumptions. Continued surveys, building on the legacy of SDSS, aim to resolve these tensions and potentially reveal new physics beyond the standard cosmological paradigm.

In summary, the synergy between theoretical models like ΛCDM and extensive observational campaigns such as SDSS has profoundly shaped our understanding of the Universe's structure and evolution, while also opening new questions that continue to drive the field of cosmology forward.

# Abstract

We present predictions for the galaxy three-point correlation function (3PCF) using high-resolution N-body simulations populated with mock galaxy catalogs constructed from halo and subhalo luminosities and colors. Using a large-volume, high-resolution dark matter simulation, we identify dark matter halos and subhalos and assign galaxy luminosities and colors via an abundance-matching technique calibrated against observed luminosity functions and color distributions from large galaxy surveys. This approach allows us to construct realistic mock galaxy catalogs without relying on semi-analytic models of galaxy formation, while still capturing the observed dependence of galaxy clustering on luminosity and color.

We measure the reduced three-point correlation function for these mock catalogs as a function of triangle shape and scale, and as a function of galaxy luminosity and color, spanning scales from the highly non-linear to quasi-linear regime. We find that the 3PCF amplitude and its configuration dependence are sensitive to both galaxy luminosity and color, with brighter and redder galaxies exhibiting different higher-order clustering signals compared to fainter, bluer populations, reflecting differences in the halo occupation distribution and small-scale galaxy assembly bias. We compare our predictions to the two-point correlation function to assess the extent to which higher-order clustering statistics provide complementary constraints on the galaxy-halo connection.

Our results demonstrate that the 3PCF, in combination with the two-point correlation function, offers powerful additional leverage for testing and constraining models of galaxy formation and evolution, disentangling degeneracies inherent in two-point statistics alone. These predictions provide a benchmark for interpreting three-point clustering measurements from ongoing and upcoming galaxy surveys, and highlight the importance of luminosity- and color-dependent higher-order statistics for extracting cosmological and astrophysical information from large-scale structure.

# Abstract

We present a measurement of the redshift-space three-point correlation function (3PCF) of dark matter halos extracted from a suite of large-volume, high-resolution N-body simulations of the concordance ΛCDM cosmology, and compare these predictions against galaxy clustering statistics derived from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) and the Two-degree Field Galaxy Redshift Survey (2dFGRS). Using halo catalogs spanning a range of mass thresholds selected to reproduce the observed galaxy number density and two-point correlation function amplitude, we compute the reduced 3PCF, Q, as a function of triangle configuration (side lengths r₁, r₂ and opening angle θ) over scales of 1–20 h⁻¹ Mpc. We find that the simulated halo 3PCF reproduces the characteristic U-shaped dependence of Q on θ observed in both SDSS and 2dFGRS data, with amplitude and shape in good agreement within the quoted uncertainties, supporting the validity of the ΛCDM structure formation paradigm and standard gravitational instability for the growth of higher-order clustering.

We further employ these measurements to test the local bias model, in which the galaxy density field is expanded as δ_g = b₁δ + (b₂/2)δ² relative to the underlying matter density field δ. By fitting the configuration dependence of Q_g to the theoretical prediction Q_g = (1/b₁)Q_m + b₂/b₁², we extract linear and nonlinear bias parameters (b₁, b₂) for both the simulated halos and the observed galaxy samples. We find that halo bias parameters depend systematically on halo mass in a manner consistent with the excursion-set/peak-background split predictions, and that the inferred b₁ and b₂ values for SDSS and 2dFGRS galaxies are consistent with those of halos in the appropriate mass range, implying near unity-to-mildly-positive linear bias and small negative nonlinear bias. However, we identify residual discrepancies in Q at the most squeezed and elongated triangle configurations, suggesting that a purely local, deterministic bias model is insufficient to fully describe the redshift-space 3PCF at small scales, and that nonlocal bias terms, scale-dependent stochasticity, or halo-occupation effects must be invoked to reconcile theory and observations. These results demonstrate the power of the 3PCF as a discriminating tool for constraining galaxy bias and testing the gravitational instability paradigm within the ΛCDM framework.

# Abstract

We investigate the dependence of the reduced three-point correlation function (Q3) on galaxy luminosity and color using high-resolution dissipationless N-body simulations combined with a halo occupation distribution (HOD) framework. By populating dark matter halos with mock galaxies according to luminosity- and color-dependent HOD models constrained by observational clustering statistics, we predict the three-point correlation function for galaxy samples spanning a range of luminosities and colors, in both real and redshift space.

Our results demonstrate that Q3 exhibits a significant dependence on both luminosity and color, with brighter and redder galaxies showing systematically different clustering amplitudes and configuration dependence compared to fainter, bluer samples. This behavior arises from the interplay between the nonlinear bias of dark matter halos and the spatial distribution of galaxies within halos, particularly the relative contributions of central and satellite galaxies to the one-halo and two-halo terms. We find that redshift-space distortions introduce additional configuration-dependent effects on Q3, modifying the real-space signal in a manner that depends sensitively on the galaxy sample's typical host halo mass and satellite fraction.

We compare our simulated predictions to measurements from large galaxy redshift surveys, finding good agreement and demonstrating that the luminosity and color dependence of Q3 provides complementary constraints on galaxy bias beyond those available from the two-point correlation function alone. In particular, we show that the three-point function breaks degeneracies inherent in two-point clustering analyses, offering tighter constraints on the relationship between galaxies and their host dark matter halos. These results highlight the diagnostic power of higher-order clustering statistics for testing and refining models of galaxy formation and evolution within the standard cosmological paradigm.

# Abstract

We present a subhalo-based mock galaxy catalog framework for investigating the dependence of the galaxy three-point correlation function (3PCF) on galaxy properties, with direct comparison to observations from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS). Using high-resolution N-body simulations, we construct mock catalogs by populating dark matter subhalos according to abundance matching and subhalo abundance matching (SHAM) prescriptions, linking galaxy luminosity, stellar mass, and color to subhalo properties such as peak circular velocity and infall mass. This approach naturally incorporates the effects of halo assembly bias and substructure dynamics on galaxy clustering statistics.

We measure the reduced 3PCF, Q(θ), and the full three-point correlation function across a range of triangle configurations and scales (1–20 h⁻¹ Mpc), examining its dependence on galaxy luminosity, color, and stellar mass. Our results demonstrate that redder, more luminous galaxies exhibit systematically stronger three-point clustering amplitudes and distinct configuration dependence compared to their blue, fainter counterparts, reflecting differences in host halo occupation and small-scale spatial distribution within halos. We find that subhalo-based mocks reproduce the luminosity and color dependence of the SDSS 3PCF significantly better than simple halo occupation distribution (HOD) models that ignore substructure information, particularly on scales below a few h⁻¹ Mpc where nonlinear clustering and satellite dynamics dominate.

Comparison with SDSS Main Galaxy Sample and luminous red galaxy samples shows good agreement in both the amplitude and shape dependence of Q(θ) as a function of galaxy subsample, validating the subhalo-based approach as a robust tool for higher-order clustering statistics. These results provide new constraints on the galaxy-halo connection and demonstrate the importance of including substructure physics when interpreting three-point clustering measurements as cosmological probes. We discuss implications for constraining galaxy formation models and testing the validity of the halo model paradigm using higher-order statistics, and outline prospects for extending this analysis to next-generation surveys such as DESI and Rubin/LSST.

# Abstract

We present an analysis of the three-point correlation function (3PCF) of dark matter halos and subhalos extracted from high-resolution cosmological N-body simulations of the ΛCDM model, aimed at resolving persistent discrepancies among previous galaxy 3PCF measurements and at testing the validity of simple, commonly-employed bias prescriptions. Measurements of the galaxy 3PCF from different redshift surveys and sample selections have historically produced inconsistent results for the reduced 3PCF amplitude Q and its dependence on triangle shape and scale, complicating efforts to constrain galaxy bias and cosmological parameters via higher-order clustering statistics. To address this, we compute the two- and three-point correlation functions of halos and subhalos as a function of mass (or circular velocity), triangle configuration, and scale, spanning the range of scales and number densities relevant to observed galaxy samples. We find that the halo/subhalo 3PCF exhibits a clear dependence on the tracer's mass or circular velocity, with more massive (or more clustered) objects displaying systematically different Q amplitudes and shape-dependences than lower-mass objects, an effect that naturally arises from the mass/velocity dependence of halo bias rather than from any additional physics. By comparing our simulation results to the published discrepant galaxy 3PCF measurements, we show that much of the apparent disagreement between studies can be attributed to differences in sample selection (e.g., luminosity or stellar-mass thresholds) that correspond to different characteristic host halo masses, rather than to observational errors or genuine anomalies in galaxy clustering. We further use the halo/subhalo 3PCF to test the standard local bias model, in which the galaxy 3PCF is related to the underlying matter 3PCF through linear and quadratic bias parameters (b1, b2). We find that while this model provides a reasonable description of the 3PCF on large, quasi-linear scales, it fails systematically at smaller scales and for certain triangle configurations, particularly for higher-mass tracers, indicating the need for scale-dependent or nonlocal bias corrections. Our results demonstrate that halo/subhalo clustering in CDM simulations can quantitatively reproduce the qualitative trends and much of the quantitative scatter seen in observational 3PCF measurements, providing a physically motivated explanation for previously unexplained discrepancies and establishing a benchmark against which future higher-order clustering measurements and bias models should be tested.
